claim: Oncogenic mutations in BRAF and NRAS occur in 70% of melanomas.
source: Oncogenic mutations in BRAF and NRAS occur in 70% of melanomas.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and introduction, citing established literature on melanoma genetics.

claim: miR-146a is highly upregulated by oncogenic BRAF and NRAS.
source: In this study, we identify a microRNA, miR-146a, that is highly upregulated by oncogenic BRAF and NRAS.
evidence: This claim is supported by deep sequencing analysis and qRT-PCR experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: Expression of miR-146a increases the ability of human melanoma cells to proliferate in culture.
source: Expression of miR-146a increases the ability of human melanoma cells to proliferate in culture and form tumors in mice, whereas knockdown of miR-146a has the opposite effects.
evidence: This is demonstrated through colony formation assays and proliferation experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Expression of miR-146a increases the ability of human melanoma cells to form tumors in mice.
source: Expression of miR-146a increases the ability of human melanoma cells to proliferate in culture and form tumors in mice, whereas knockdown of miR-146a has the opposite effects.
evidence: This is supported by xenograft experiments in nude mice shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Knockdown of miR-146a decreases the ability of human melanoma cells to proliferate in culture and form tumors in mice.
source: Expression of miR-146a increases the ability of human melanoma cells to proliferate in culture and form tumors in mice, whereas knockdown of miR-146a has the opposite effects.
evidence: This is demonstrated through miRZip-146a experiments shown in Figure 3D-G.

claim: miR-146a targets the NUMB mRNA.
source: We show these oncogenic activities are due to miR-146a targeting the NUMB mRNA, a repressor of Notch signaling.
evidence: This is supported by microarray analysis, luciferase reporter assays, and Western blot analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: NUMB is a repressor of Notch signaling.
source: We show these oncogenic activities are due to miR-146a targeting the NUMB mRNA, a repressor of Notch signaling.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field and supported by the functional experiments in the study.

claim: pre-miR-146a contains a single nucleotide polymorphism (C>G rs2910164).
source: Previous studies have shown that pre-miR-146a contains a single nucleotide polymorphism (C>G rs2910164).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature and confirmed by sequencing in this study.

claim: The ability of pre-miR-146a/G to activate Notch signaling is substantially higher than that of pre-miR-146a/C.
source: We find that the ability of pre-miR-146a/G to activate Notch signaling and promote oncogenesis is substantially higher than that of pre-miR-146a/C.
evidence: This is demonstrated through CSL-Luciferase reporter assays and Notch target gene expression analysis shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: The ability of pre-miR-146a/G to promote oncogenesis is substantially higher than that of pre-miR-146a/C.
source: We find that the ability of pre-miR-146a/G to activate Notch signaling and promote oncogenesis is substantially higher than that of pre-miR-146a/C.
evidence: This is supported by colony formation assays, soft-agar assays, and tumor formation experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: During melanoma progression pre-miR-146a/G is enriched relative to pre-miR-146a/C.
source: Analysis of melanoma cell lines and matched patient samples indicates that during melanoma progression pre-miR-146a/G is enriched relative to pre-miR-146a/C, resulting from a C-to-G somatic mutation in pre-miR-146a/C.
evidence: This is demonstrated through sequencing of matched patient samples shown in Table 1.

claim: Enrichment of pre-miR-146a/G during melanoma progression results from a C-to-G somatic mutation in pre-miR-146a/C.
source: Analysis of melanoma cell lines and matched patient samples indicates that during melanoma progression pre-miR-146a/G is enriched relative to pre-miR-146a/C, resulting from a C-to-G somatic mutation in pre-miR-146a/C.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of matched patient samples where pre-miR-146a/C in earlier stages becomes pre-miR-146a/G in later stages.

claim: Melanoma is the deadliest form of skin cancer accounting for ∼80% of skin cancer-related deaths.
source: Melanoma is the deadliest form of skin cancer accounting for ∼80% of skin cancer-related deaths (Miller and Mihm, 2006).
evidence: This is cited from Miller and Mihm, 2006.

claim: Activating mutations in the BRAF and NRAS proto-oncogenes occur in 70% of melanoma cases.
source: The most commonly observed oncogenic events in melanomas are activating mutations in the BRAF and NRAS proto-oncogenes, which occur in 70% of cases (Miller and Mihm, 2006; Tsao et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from Miller and Mihm, 2006 and Tsao et al., 2012.

claim: Activating mutations in BRAF and NRAS genes cause constitutive activation of downstream signaling pathways.
source: Activating mutations in BRAF and NRAS genes cause constitutive activation of downstream signaling pathways, resulting in pro-proliferative and anti-apoptotic effects that promote cellular transformation, tumor growth and metastasis (Downward, 2003; Wellbrock et al., 2004; Karnoub and Weinberg, 2008).
evidence: This is cited from Downward, 2003; Wellbrock et al., 2004; Karnoub and Weinberg, 2008.

claim: Oncogenic BRAF mutants (typically BRAFV600E) primarily activate the MAPK pathway.
source: Oncogenic BRAF mutants (typically BRAFV600E) primarily activate the MAPK pathway (Wellbrock et al., 2004).
evidence: This is cited from Wellbrock et al., 2004.

claim: Disruption of the BRAF-MEK-ERK pathway blocks the growth of melanoma cells harboring an oncogenic BRAF mutation.
source: Genetic and pharmacological studies have shown that disruption of the BRAF-MEK-ERK pathway blocks the growth of melanoma cells harboring an oncogenic BRAF mutation and thus represents an attractive therapeutic target (Wellbrock et al., 2004; Miller and Mihm, 2006; Tsao et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from Wellbrock et al., 2004; Miller and Mihm, 2006; Tsao et al., 2012.

claim: Oncogenic NRAS is capable of activating multiple downstream pathways, including BRAF-MEK-ERK.
source: Oncogenic NRAS is capable of activating multiple downstream pathways, including BRAF-MEK-ERK, all of which are thought to play an important role in NRAS driven oncogenesis (Downward, 2003; Karnoub and Weinberg, 2008).
evidence: This is cited from Downward, 2003; Karnoub and Weinberg, 2008.

claim: The Notch pathway is an evolutionary conserved signaling cascade that has an essential role in embryonic development and cell renewal in the adult.
source: The Notch pathway is an evolutionary conserved signaling cascade that has an essential role in embryonic development and cell renewal in the adult (Guruharsha et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from Guruharsha et al., 2012.

claim: Notch signaling has a key role in melanoblast and melanocyte homeostasis.
source: Notch signaling has a key role in melanoblast and melanocyte homeostasis (Haass and Herlyn, 2005; Aubin-Houzelstein et al., 2008; Kumano et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from Haass and Herlyn, 2005; Aubin-Houzelstein et al., 2008; Kumano et al., 2008.

claim: Conditional ablation of Notch signaling in the melanocyte lineage leads to drastic elimination of melanoblasts and melanocyte stem cells.
source: For example, conditional ablation of Notch signaling in the melanocyte lineage leads to drastic elimination of melanoblasts and melanocyte stem cells (Moriyama et al., 2006).
evidence: This is cited from Moriyama et al., 2006.

claim: NOTCH1 expression is normally decreased in mature melanocytes.
source: NOTCH1 expression is normally decreased in mature melanocytes, whereas melanomas regain expression and activity of NOTCH1 (Balint et al., 2005; Pinnix et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited from Balint et al., 2005; Pinnix et al., 2009.

claim: Melanomas regain expression and activity of NOTCH1.
source: NOTCH1 expression is normally decreased in mature melanocytes, whereas melanomas regain expression and activity of NOTCH1 (Balint et al., 2005; Pinnix et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited from Balint et al., 2005; Pinnix et al., 2009.

claim: NOTCH1 is required for melanoma formation.
source: NOTCH1 is required for melanoma formation, can transform primary human melanocytes and can confer metastatic properties to primary melanoma cells (Liu et al., 2006; Asnaghi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from Liu et al., 2006; Asnaghi et al., 2012.

claim: NOTCH1 can transform primary human melanocytes.
source: NOTCH1 is required for melanoma formation, can transform primary human melanocytes and can confer metastatic properties to primary melanoma cells (Liu et al., 2006; Asnaghi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from Liu et al., 2006; Asnaghi et al., 2012.

claim: NOTCH1 can confer metastatic properties to primary melanoma cells.
source: NOTCH1 is required for melanoma formation, can transform primary human melanocytes and can confer metastatic properties to primary melanoma cells (Liu et al., 2006; Asnaghi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from Liu et al., 2006; Asnaghi et al., 2012.

claim: miRNAs are small non-coding RNAs that function by regulating the stability or translation of mRNAs.
source: miRNAs are small non-coding RNAs that function by regulating the stability or translation of mRNAs (Bartel, 2004; He and Hannon, 2004; Leung and Sharp, 2006).
evidence: This is cited from Bartel, 2004; He and Hannon, 2004; Leung and Sharp, 2006.

claim: miRNAs have been implicated in essentially all aspects of tumor biology including tumorigenesis, angiogenesis and metastasis.
source: miRNAs have been implicated in essentially all aspects of tumor biology including tumorigenesis, angiogenesis and metastasis (Croce, 2009; Garzon et al., 2009) indicating that, similar to protein-coding genes, miRNAs function as crucial regulators of tumor initiation and progression.
evidence: This is cited from Croce, 2009; Garzon et al., 2009.

claim: miRNAs can act as either tumor suppressors or oncogenes depending on the functions of their targets.
source: Interestingly, miRNAs can act as either tumor suppressors or oncogenes depending on the functions of their targets (Croce, 2009; Garzon et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited from Croce, 2009; Garzon et al., 2009.

claim: More than half of miRNA genes in human cancers are located in chromosomal regions that frequently exhibit amplification, deletion, or translocation.
source: For example, more than half of miRNA genes in human cancers are located in chromosomal regions that frequently exhibit amplification, deletion, or translocation (Croce, 2009; Garzon et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited from Croce, 2009; Garzon et al., 2009.

claim: miR-146a was identified as the most upregulated miRNA by BRAFV600E through deep sequencing analysis.
source: Our analysis identified miR-146a as the most upregulated miRNA by BRAFV600E (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the volcano plot in Figure 1B showing miR-146a as the most significantly upregulated miRNA.

claim: BRAFV600E activates miR-146a expression in WI-38, IMR-90, and primary human melanocytes.
source: We found that BRAFV600E activates miR-146a expression in WI-38 as well as in IMR-90 and melanocytes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown by qRT-PCR analysis in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Treatment of MEL-ST/BRAFV600E cells with the MEK inhibitor U0216 results in decreased miR-146a expression.
source: Figure 1D shows that treatment of MEL-ST/BRAFV600E cells with U0216 resulted in decreased miR-146a expression.
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR analysis in Figure 1D.

claim: Stable expression of NRASQ61K results in increased miR-146a levels.
source: Similar to BRAFV600E, stable expression of NRASQ61K, HRAS v12 or a mutant that selectively activates BRAF-MEK-ERK signaling also resulted in increased miR-146a levels (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 3), which was attenuated by addition of U0216 (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is shown by qRT-PCR analysis in Figure 1E.

claim: Expression of constitutively active MEK (MEK DD) substantially increased BRAF-MEK-ERK signaling and stimulated miR-146a expression.
source: Figure 1F shows that expression of MEK DD substantially increased BRAF-MEK-ERK signaling and stimulated miR-146a expression.
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR and immunoblot analysis in Figure 1F.

claim: miR-146a expression was significantly higher in a subset of BRAF and NRAS mutant melanoma cell lines compared to both BRAF/NRAS wild-type melanoma cell lines and melanocytes.
source: Figure 1G shows that miR-146a expression was significantly higher in a subset of BRAF and NRAS mutant melanoma cell lines compared to both BRAF/NRAS wild-type melanoma cell lines and melanocytes.
evidence: This is shown by qRT-PCR analysis in Figure 1G.

claim: BRAF-MEK-ERK signaling is necessary for miR-146a upregulation.
source: Collectively, our results show that BRAF-MEK-ERK signaling is necessary and increased BRAF-MEK-ERK signaling is sufficient for upregulation of miR-146a.
evidence: This is inferred from the experiments showing that MEK inhibition reduces miR-146a expression.

claim: Increased BRAF-MEK-ERK signaling is sufficient for upregulation of miR-146a.
source: Collectively, our results show that BRAF-MEK-ERK signaling is necessary and increased BRAF-MEK-ERK signaling is sufficient for upregulation of miR-146a.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experiments showing that expression of constitutively active MEK increases miR-146a expression.

claim: The BRAF-MEK-ERK pathway regulates transcription, protein stability and activity of MYC.
source: Several previous studies have shown that the BRAF-MEK-ERK pathway regulates transcription, protein stability and activity of MYC (Sears et al., 1999, 2000; Pintus et al., 2002; Marampon et al., 2006; Tsai et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from Sears et al., 1999, 2000; Pintus et al., 2002; Marampon et al., 2006; Tsai et al., 2012.

claim: The miR-146a promoter contains a potential MYC binding site.
source: Analysis of the miR-146a promoter sequence using the PROMO 3.0 bioinformatics program (Messeguer et al., 2002) identified a potential MYC binding site (Figure 2A), suggesting that MYC promotes miR-146a upregulation.
evidence: This is shown by bioinformatics analysis and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: Stable expression of BRAFV600E in MEL-ST cells led to increased MYC expression and increased MYC phosphorylation.
source: Stable expression of BRAFV600E in MEL-ST cells led to increased MYC expression, increased MYC phosphorylation (Figure 2B) and, as monitored in a chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assay, binding of MYC to the miR-146a promoter (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot analysis in Figure 2B.

claim: Stable expression of BRAFV600E in MEL-ST cells led to binding of MYC to the miR-146a promoter.
source: Stable expression of BRAFV600E in MEL-ST cells led to increased MYC expression, increased MYC phosphorylation (Figure 2B) and, as monitored in a chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assay, binding of MYC to the miR-146a promoter (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP assay in Figure 2C.

claim: Binding of MYC to miR-146a promoter was inhibited by the treatment of cells with U0216.
source: Notably, binding of MYC to miR-146a promoter was inhibited by the treatment of cells with U0216 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP assay in Figure 2C.

claim: shRNA-mediated knockdown of MYC in melanoma cell lines SKMEL-28 and M14 substantially decreased miR-146a levels.
source: Furthermore, shRNA-mediated knockdown of MYC in melanoma cell lines, SKMEL-28 and M14, substantially decreased miR-146a levels and the expression of other MYC target genes (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR analysis in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3.

claim: shRNA-mediated knockdown of MYC resulted in decreased binding of MYC to the miR-146a promoter.
source: As expected, shRNA-mediated knockdown of MYC also resulted in decreased binding of MYC to the miR-146a promoter (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP assay in Figure 2E.

claim: Increased BRAF-MEK-ERK signaling results in activation and recruitment of MYC to the miR-146a promoter, which stimulates miR-146a transcription.
source: Collectively, our results show that increased BRAF-MEK-ERK signaling results in activation and recruitment of MYC to the miR-146a promoter, which stimulates miR-146a transcription.
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP and knockdown experiments showing MYC binding and its requirement for miR-146a expression.

claim: The amount of mature miR-146a produced from pre-miR-146a/G was higher than that from pre-miR-146a/C.
source: Significantly, consistent with a previous report (Jazdzewski et al., 2008), the amount of mature miR-146a produced from pre-miR-146a/G was higher than that from pre-miR-146a/C (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and is consistent with previous literature.

claim: Ectopic expression of pre-miR-146a/G promoted proliferation at a higher rate than pre-miR-146a/C in two of the three melanoma cell lines analyzed.
source: Ectopic expression of pre-miR-146a/G promoted proliferation at a higher rate than pre-miR-146a/C, as evidenced by increased colony formation and increased proliferation in two of the three melanoma cell lines analyzed (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by colony formation and proliferation assays in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: pre-miR-146a/G stimulated colony formation in soft-agar more efficiently than pre-miR-146a/C.
source: Again, pre-miR-146a/G-stimulated colony formation more efficiently than pre-miR-146a/C (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by soft-agar assays in Figure 3C.

claim: Inhibition of miR-146a by miRZip-146a in SKMEL-28 and M14 cells reduced colony formation in liquid culture and soft-agar.
source: Conversely, inhibition of miR-146a by miRZip-146a in SKMEL-28 and M14 cells reduced colony formation in liquid culture and soft-agar, and inhibited tumor formation in mice (Figure 3D–G and Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by colony formation and soft-agar assays in Figure 3D-F and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Inhibition of miR-146a by miRZip-146a in SKMEL-28 and M14 cells inhibited tumor formation in mice.
source: Conversely, inhibition of miR-146a by miRZip-146a in SKMEL-28 and M14 cells reduced colony formation in liquid culture and soft-agar, and inhibited tumor formation in mice (Figure 3D–G and Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by xenograft experiments in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Both pre-miR-146a/C and pre-miR146a/G enhanced tumor growth in mice, but the effect was much larger with pre-miR-146a/G.
source: Although both pre-miR-146a/C and pre-miR146a/G enhanced tumor growth, the effect was much larger with pre-miR-146a/G (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by xenograft experiments in Figure 3H.

claim: Increased levels of miR-146a enhanced proliferation in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Notably, increased levels of miR-146a enhanced proliferation in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 3—figure supplements 7 and 8).
evidence: This is demonstrated by transfection of synthetic miR-146a at increasing concentrations in Figure 3—figure supplements 7 and 8.

claim: The oncogenic activity of pre-miR-146a/G is greater than that of pre-miR-146a/C both in vitro and in vivo due to increased abundance of mature miR-146a.
source: Collectively, our results show that the oncogenic activity of pre-miR-146a/G is greater than that of pre-miR-146a/C both in vitro and in vivo due to increased abundance of mature miR-146a.
evidence: This is inferred from the experiments showing higher mature miR-146a levels from pre-miR-146a/G and its greater oncogenic effects.

claim: BRAFV600E was not sufficient to transform immortalized MEL-ST melanocytes.
source: In agreement with a previous report (Chudnovsky et al., 2005), we found that BRAFV600E was not sufficient to transform the immortalized melanocytes (Figure 3—figure supplement 9).
evidence: This is demonstrated by soft-agar assays in Figure 3—figure supplement 9 and is consistent with previous literature.

claim: Inhibition of miR-146a expression substantially reduced the ability of NRASQ61K-expressing cells to form colonies in soft-agar.
source: Notably, inhibition of miR-146a expression substantially reduced the ability of NRASQ61K-expressing cells to form colonies in soft-agar (Figure 3I) and tumors in mice (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by soft-agar assays in Figure 3I.

claim: Inhibition of miR-146a expression substantially reduced the ability of NRASQ61K-expressing cells to form tumors in mice.
source: Notably, inhibition of miR-146a expression substantially reduced the ability of NRASQ61K-expressing cells to form colonies in soft-agar (Figure 3I) and tumors in mice (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by xenograft experiments in Figure 3J.

claim: miR-146a promotes the initiation and progression of melanoma.
source: Collectively, our results show that miR-146a promotes the initiation and progression of melanoma.
evidence: This is inferred from the multiple experiments showing that miR-146a enhances proliferation, colony formation, and tumor growth.

claim: TargetScan analysis identified 20 mRNAs with potential miR-146a binding sites in the 3′-UTR among genes downregulated by both pre-miR-146a/C and pre-miR-146a/G.
source: Of the genes downregulated by both pre-miR-146a/C and pre-miR-146a/G, TargetScan analysis identified 20 mRNAs with potential miR-146a binding sites in the 3′-UTR (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is based on microarray analysis and bioinformatics prediction using TargetScan.

claim: NUMB mRNA encodes a repressor of NOTCH.
source: We elected to focus on the NUMB mRNA because it encodes a repressor of NOTCH and several previous studies have shown that NOTCH functions as an oncogene in melanoma (Liu et al., 2006; Pinnix et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Liu et al., 2006; Pinnix et al., 2009.

claim: Candidate miR-146a binding sites were identified in both the 3′ UTR and coding region of NUMB mRNA.
source: We identified candidate miR-146a binding sites in both the 3′ UTR and coding region of NUMB mRNA (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown by sequence analysis illustrated in Figure 4A.

claim: pre-miR-146a/G decreased NUMB mRNA and protein levels more efficiently than pre-miR-146a/C.
source: Consistent with its increased oncogenic activity, pre-miR-146a/G decreased NUMB mRNA and protein levels more efficiently than pre-miR-146a/C (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR and immunoblot analysis in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: miR-146a does not target the site within the NUMB 3′-UTR.
source: Using a luciferase reporter assay, we found that miR-146a does not target the site within the NUMB 3′-UTR (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase reporter assay in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Ectopic expression of miR-146a downregulated the expression of wild-type NUMB (NUMB-WT) open reading frame (ORF).
source: By contrast, ectopic expression of miR-146a downregulated the expression of wild-type NUMB (NUMB-WT) open reading frame (ORF), whereas expression of a miR-146a-resistant NUMB ORF (NUMB-MUT) lacking the binding site in the coding region was unaffected (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis in Figure 4C.

claim: Expression of a miR-146a-resistant NUMB ORF (NUMB-MUT) lacking the binding site in the coding region was unaffected by miR-146a.
source: By contrast, ectopic expression of miR-146a downregulated the expression of wild-type NUMB (NUMB-WT) open reading frame (ORF), whereas expression of a miR-146a-resistant NUMB ORF (NUMB-MUT) lacking the binding site in the coding region was unaffected (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis in Figure 4C.

claim: Both pre-miR-146a/C and pre-miR-146a/G stimulated CSL-Luc activity but the effect was greater with pre-miR-146a/G.
source: Notably, both pre-miR-146a/C- and pre-miR-146a/G-stimulated CSL-Luc activity but again the effect was greater with pre-miR-146a/G (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by dual luciferase assay in Figure 4D.

claim: Notch signaling targets were upregulated to a greater extent by pre-miR-146a/G compared to pre-miR-146a/C.
source: In agreement with the reporter assays, we found that Notch signaling targets were upregulated to a greater extent by pre-miR-146a/G compared to pre-miR-146a/C (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR analysis of Notch target genes in Figure 4E.

claim: Stable knockdown of miR-146a decreased CSL-Luc activity.
source: Conversely, stable knockdown of miR-146a decreased CSL-Luc activity and reduced Notch target gene expression (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by dual luciferase assay in Figure 4F.

claim: Stable knockdown of miR-146a reduced Notch target gene expression.
source: Conversely, stable knockdown of miR-146a decreased CSL-Luc activity and reduced Notch target gene expression (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR analysis in Figure 4G.

claim: NUMB is a direct target of miR-146a.
source: Collectively, these results confirm that NUMB is a direct target of miR-146a and that miR-146a downregulates NUMB to activate Notch signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the experiments showing miR-146a binding to NUMB coding region and its effects on NUMB expression.

claim: miR-146a downregulates NUMB to activate Notch signaling.
source: Collectively, these results confirm that NUMB is a direct target of miR-146a and that miR-146a downregulates NUMB to activate Notch signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the experiments showing that miR-146a reduces NUMB expression and increases Notch signaling.

claim: Depletion of NUMB increased cellular proliferation in SKMEL-28 cells.
source: Similar to ectopic expression of miR-146a, depletion of NUMB increased cellular proliferation (Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2), soft-agar colony formation (Figure 5B) and tumor formation in mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by proliferation assays in Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: Depletion of NUMB increased soft-agar colony formation in SKMEL-28 cells.
source: Similar to ectopic expression of miR-146a, depletion of NUMB increased cellular proliferation (Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2), soft-agar colony formation (Figure 5B) and tumor formation in mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by soft-agar assays in Figure 5B.

claim: Depletion of NUMB increased tumor formation in mice.
source: Similar to ectopic expression of miR-146a, depletion of NUMB increased cellular proliferation (Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2), soft-agar colony formation (Figure 5B) and tumor formation in mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by xenograft experiments in Figure 5C.

claim: Ectopic expression of activated intracellular NOTCH1 (ICN) enhanced cellular proliferation in liquid culture.
source: As predicted, ectopic expression of ICN-enhanced cellular proliferation in liquid culture (Figure 5—figure supplements 3 and 4), colony formation in soft-agar (Figure 5E) and tumor formation in mice (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by proliferation assays in Figure 5—figure supplements 3 and 4.

claim: Ectopic expression of activated intracellular NOTCH1 (ICN) enhanced colony formation in soft-agar.
source: As predicted, ectopic expression of ICN-enhanced cellular proliferation in liquid culture (Figure 5—figure supplements 3 and 4), colony formation in soft-agar (Figure 5E) and tumor formation in mice (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by soft-agar assays in Figure 5E.

claim: Ectopic expression of activated intracellular NOTCH1 (ICN) enhanced tumor formation in mice.
source: As predicted, ectopic expression of ICN-enhanced cellular proliferation in liquid culture (Figure 5—figure supplements 3 and 4), colony formation in soft-agar (Figure 5E) and tumor formation in mice (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by xenograft experiments in Figure 5F.

claim: Expression of NUMB-MUT, but not NUMB-WT, prevented pre-miR-146a/G from promoting colony formation in soft-agar.
source: We found that the expression of NUMB-MUT, but not NUMB-WT, prevented pre-miR-146a/G from promoting colony formation in soft-agar (Figure 5G) and activating NOTCH signaling (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by soft-agar assays in Figure 5G.

claim: Expression of NUMB-MUT, but not NUMB-WT, prevented pre-miR-146a/G from activating NOTCH signaling.
source: We found that the expression of NUMB-MUT, but not NUMB-WT, prevented pre-miR-146a/G from promoting colony formation in soft-agar (Figure 5G) and activating NOTCH signaling (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR analysis of Notch target genes in Figure 5H.

claim: NUMB-MUT, but not NUMB-WT blocked the ability of NRASQ61K transformed MEL-ST cells to form colonies in soft-agar.
source: Moreover, NUMB-MUT, but not NUMB-WT blocked the ability of NRASQ61K transformed MEL-ST cells to form colonies in soft-agar (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by soft-agar assays in Figure 5I.

claim: Simultaneous antagonism of miR-146a and knockdown of NUMB restored proliferation of SKMEL-28 and M14 cells in both liquid culture and soft-agar.
source: Notably, simultaneous antagonism of miR-146a and knockdown of NUMB restored proliferation of SKMEL-28 and M14 cells in both liquid culture and soft-agar (Figure 5J–M).
evidence: This is demonstrated by colony formation and soft-agar assays in Figure 5J-M.

claim: Combined U0216 and DAPT treatment inhibited proliferation of SKMEL-28 and SKMEL-19 cells much strongly than either of the drugs alone.
source: Notably, combined U0216 and DAPT treatment inhibited proliferation of SKMEL-28 and SKMEL-19 cells much strongly than either of the drugs alone (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MTT proliferation assays in Figure 6A.

claim: U0216 efficiently blocked MAPK signaling in SKMEL-28 and SKMEL-19 cells.
source: As expected, U0216 efficiently blocked MAPK signaling (Figure 6B) and DAPT inhibited the transcriptional targets of Notch signaling (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot analysis in Figure 6B.

claim: DAPT inhibited the transcriptional targets of Notch signaling in SKMEL-28 and SKMEL-19 cells.
source: As expected, U0216 efficiently blocked MAPK signaling (Figure 6B) and DAPT inhibited the transcriptional targets of Notch signaling (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR analysis in Figure 6C.

claim: The ability of miR-146a to block NUMB expression and activate Notch signaling is necessary for miR-146a to promote melanoma initiation and progression.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that the ability of miR-146a to block NUMB expression and activate Notch signaling is necessary for miR-146a to promote melanoma initiation and progression.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments showing that NUMB-MUT blocks miR-146a's oncogenic effects.

claim: Two out of three melanocytes were homozygous for pre-miR-146a/C.
source: We found that two out of three melanocytes were homozygous for pre-miR-146a/C and one was a pre-miR-146a/C:pre-miR-146a/G heterozygote.
evidence: This is based on sequencing of genomic DNA from melanocyte cultures.

claim: One out of three melanocytes was a pre-miR-146a/C:pre-miR-146a/G heterozygote.
source: We found that two out of three melanocytes were homozygous for pre-miR-146a/C and one was a pre-miR-146a/C:pre-miR-146a/G heterozygote.
evidence: This is based on sequencing of genomic DNA from melanocyte cultures.

claim: All melanoma cell lines were either pre-miR-146a/C:pre-miR-146a/G heterozygotes or pre-miR-146a/G homozygotes.
source: By contrast, all melanoma cell lines were either pre-miR-146a/C:pre-miR-146a/G heterozygotes or pre-miR-146a/G homozygotes (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on sequencing of genomic DNA from melanoma cell lines shown in Table 1.

claim: In 4 of 10 cases the nevus contains a pre-miR-146a/C allele that is a pre-miR-146a/G allele in the matched primary melanoma.
source: As shown in Table 1, in 4 of 10 cases the nevus contains a pre-miR-146a/C allele that is a pre-miR-146a/G allele in the matched primary melanoma.
evidence: This is based on sequencing of matched patient samples shown in Table 1.

claim: In 8 of 15 cases analyzed, a pre-miR-146a/C allele in the primary melanoma is a pre-miR-146a/G allele in the matched metastases.
source: Remarkably, in 8 of 15 cases analyzed, a pre-miR-146a/C allele in the primary melanoma is a pre-miR-146a/G allele in the matched metastases.
evidence: This is based on sequencing of matched patient samples shown in Table 1.

claim: In one case, both pre-miR-146a/C alleles in the primary melanoma are pre-miR-146a/G alleles in the matched metastasis.
source: In one case, both pre-miR-146a/C alleles in the primary melanoma are pre-miR-146a/G alleles in the matched metastasis.
evidence: This is based on sequencing of matched patient samples shown in Table 1.

claim: There is a selection for pre-miR-146a/G during melanoma progression.
source: Collectively, these results reveal a selection for pre-miR-146a/G during melanoma progression.
evidence: This is inferred from the enrichment of pre-miR-146a/G in more advanced melanoma stages.

claim: Enrichment of pre-miR-146a/G results from a C-to-G mutation in pre-miR-146a.
source: Moreover, the results with matched patient samples indicate that enrichment of pre-miR-146a/G results from a C-to-G mutation in pre-miR-146a.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that pre-miR-146a/C in earlier stages becomes pre-miR-146a/G in later stages in matched samples.

claim: miR-146a has a critical role in the initiation and progression of BRAF/NRAS-positive melanomas.
source: In this report, we demonstrate a critical role for miR-146a in the initiation and progression of BRAF/NRAS-positive melanomas, which is summarized in Figure 6D and discussed below.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all the experimental data.

claim: Upregulation of miR-146a by activated BRAF, as well as activated NRAS, occurs through the MAPK signaling pathway.
source: Upregulation of miR-146a by activated BRAF, as well as activated NRAS, occurs through the MAPK signaling pathway.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experiments showing that MEK inhibition blocks miR-146a upregulation.

claim: BRAF and NRAS mutant melanoma cell lines and short-term melanoma cultures show higher levels of miR-146a compared to those that are wild type for these genes.
source: Accordingly, we find that BRAF and NRAS mutant melanoma cell lines and short-term melanoma cultures show higher levels of miR-146a compared to those that are wild type for these genes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR analysis in Figure 1G.

claim: The MAPK pathway regulates the phosphorylation of the transcription factor MYC.
source: We show that the MAPK pathway regulates the phosphorylation of the transcription factor MYC, which in turn binds to the promoter of miR-146a and stimulates its transcription.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot and ChIP experiments in Figure 2.

claim: MYC binds to the promoter of miR-146a and stimulates its transcription.
source: We show that the MAPK pathway regulates the phosphorylation of the transcription factor MYC, which in turn binds to the promoter of miR-146a and stimulates its transcription.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP and knockdown experiments in Figure 2.

claim: MYC has been found to stimulate transcription of several other miRNAs.
source: Notably, MYC has been found to stimulate transcription of several other miRNAs (Chang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from Chang et al., 2008.

claim: MYC has been shown to directly activate transcription of the oncogenic miR-17-92 cluster.
source: For example, MYC has been shown to directly activate transcription of the oncogenic miR-17-92 cluster and thereby promote cell proliferation, survival, angiogenesis, and metabolic reprogramming in a number of tumor cell lines (Mu et al., 2009; Dews et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Mu et al., 2009; Dews et al., 2010.

claim: miRNAs and components of miRNA biogenesis pathways such as Dicer have been implicated in several aspects of melanocyte biology as well as in melanoma initiation and progression.
source: miRNAs and components of miRNA biogenesis pathways such as Dicer have been implicated in several aspects of melanocyte biology as well as in melanoma initiation and progression (Levy et al., 2010; Bonazzi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from Levy et al., 2010; Bonazzi et al., 2012.

claim: Previous studies have shown that miR-146a can function either as an oncogene or as a tumor suppressor depending upon the cell type.
source: Previous studies have shown that miR-146a can function either as an oncogene or as a tumor suppressor depending upon the cell type (Boldin et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from Boldin et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2013.

claim: miR-146a has been shown to function as an oncogene in papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC), triple negative sporadic breast cancers and anaplastic thyroid carcinoma.
source: For example, miR-146a has been shown to function as an oncogene in a variety of human cancers including papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC), triple negative sporadic breast cancers and anaplastic thyroid carcinoma (Jazdzewski et al., 2008; Pacifico et al., 2010; Garcia et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from Jazdzewski et al., 2008; Pacifico et al., 2010; Garcia et al., 2011.

claim: miR-146a was previously reported to target NUMB mRNA in mouse myocytes C2C12 cells.
source: Consistent, with our results, miR-146a was previously reported to target NUMB mRNA in mouse myocytes C2C12 cells (Kuang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited from Kuang et al., 2009.

claim: NUMB targeting and activation of Notch signaling was necessary for the ability of miR-146a to promote the initiation and progression of melanoma.
source: We confirmed NUMB as a direct target of miR-146a and showed that NUMB targeting and activation of Notch signaling was necessary for the ability of miR-146a to promote the initiation and progression of melanoma.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the rescue experiments with NUMB-MUT.

claim: Many cancers, including melanoma, have been found to have increased Notch signaling.
source: Many cancers, including melanoma, have been found to have increased Notch signaling, which results from two distinct mechanisms (Ranganathan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from Ranganathan et al., 2011.

claim: Gain-of-function mutations in NOTCH1 can increase Notch signaling.
source: First, gain-of-function mutations in NOTCH1 can increase Notch signaling (Ranganathan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from Ranganathan et al., 2011.

claim: Decreased expression of NUMB can result in increased Notch signaling.
source: Second, decreased expression of NUMB can result in increased Notch signaling (Guo et al., 1996).
evidence: This is cited from Guo et al., 1996.

claim: NUMB expression is decreased in breast and lung cancer.
source: For example, NUMB expression is decreased in breast and lung cancer and NUMB is considered to be a tumor suppressor in these malignancies (Lindsay et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from Lindsay et al., 2008.

claim: NUMB is considered to be a tumor suppressor in breast and lung cancer.
source: For example, NUMB expression is decreased in breast and lung cancer and NUMB is considered to be a tumor suppressor in these malignancies (Lindsay et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from Lindsay et al., 2008.

claim: Notch signaling can be increased by upregulation of a miRNAs that targets NUMB.
source: In this study, we have shown that Notch signaling can also be increased by upregulation of a miRNAs that targets NUMB.
evidence: This is the novel mechanism demonstrated in this study.

claim: The oncogenic activity of pre-miR-146a/G is substantially greater than that of pre-miR-146a/C, which results, at least in part, from more efficient processing of pre-miR-146a/G compared to pre-miR-146a/C.
source: We found that the oncogenic activity of pre-miR-146a/G is substantially greater than that of pre-miR-146a/C, which results, at least in part, from more efficient processing of pre-miR-146a/G compared to pre-miR-146a/C.
evidence: This is inferred from the experiments showing higher mature miR-146a levels from pre-miR-146a/G.

claim: pre-miR-146a/G undergoes a more efficient nuclear processing compared to pre-miR-146a/C and thus give rise to a higher amount of mature miR-146a.
source: Our results are consistent with a previous report showing that pre-miR-146a/G undergoes a more efficient nuclear processing compared to pre-miR-146a/C and thus give rise to a higher amount of mature miR-146a (Jazdzewski et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from Jazdzewski et al., 2008 and is consistent with the data in this study.

claim: Analysis of melanoma cell lines and matched patient samples reveal enrichment of the more oncogenic variant, pre-miR-146a/G, during melanoma progression.
source: Most importantly, our analysis of melanoma cell lines and matched patient samples of nevi, primary, and metastatic melanoma reveal enrichment of the more oncogenic variant, pre-miR-146a/G, during melanoma progression.
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequencing of matched patient samples shown in Table 1.

claim: The results are consistent with previous studies that observed enrichment for pre-miR-146a/G during melanoma progression.
source: Our results are consistent with previous studies that observed enrichment for pre-miR-146a/G (Gast et al., 2010; Supplementary file 1D) and increased miR-146a expression (Philippidou et al., 2010) during melanoma progression.
evidence: This is cited from Gast et al., 2010 and Philippidou et al., 2010.

claim: Both the Notch and BRAF-MEK-ERK signaling pathways are amenable to pharmacological inhibition.
source: Both the Notch and BRAF-MEK-ERK signaling pathways are amenable to pharmacological inhibition (Rizzo et al., 2008; Bollag et al., 2010; Flaherty et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Rizzo et al., 2008; Bollag et al., 2010; Flaherty et al., 2010.

claim: Combining clinically approved γ–secretase inhibitors with BRAF inhibitors might be a more effective treatment of BRAF/NRAS mutant melanomas.
source: Our results suggest that combining clinically approved γ–secretase inhibitors, which block Notch activation, with BRAF inhibitors, which block BRAF-MEK-ERK signaling, might be a more effective treatment of BRAF/NRAS mutant melanomas.
evidence: This is suggested based on the synergistic effects of combined U0216 and DAPT treatment shown in Figure 6A.

claim: NUMB negatively regulates NOTCH, potentially through a direct protein–protein interaction that requires the phosphotyrosine-binding (PTB) domain of NUMB and either the RAM23 region or the very C-terminal end of NOTCH.
source: It is thought that NUMB negatively regulates NOTCH, potentially through a direct protein–protein interaction that requires the phosphotyrosine-binding (PTB) domain of NUMB and either the RAM23 region or the very C-terminal end of NOTCH (Guo et al., 1996).
evidence: This is cited from Guo et al., 1996.

claim: MEL-ST cells are immortalized melanocytes that have basal levels of BRAF-MEK-ERK signaling and can be transformed by single oncogenes.
source: We stably expressed BRAFV600E or an empty vector in MEL-ST cells, which are immortalized melanocytes that have basal levels of BRAF-MEK-ERK signaling and can be transformed by single oncogenes (Gupta et al., 2005).
evidence: This is cited from Gupta et al., 2005.

claim: Over 60% of melanomas harbor mutations in the BRAF and NRAS genes.
source: Over 60% of melanomas harbor mutations in the BRAF and NRAS genes (Davies et al., 2002; Chin et al., 2006).
evidence: This is cited from Davies et al., 2002; Chin et al., 2006.
